top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: the finding of entropy-driven reversible exsolution/dissolution in high-entropy catalysts (PMC8505510::web::010, PMC8505510::web::015) by proposing a surface engineering approach that works in tandem with these intrinsic dynamics.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a carefully engineered, oxygen-ion–conducting overcoat that is specifically tailored to interact with the high-entropy substrate’s dynamic oxygen vacancy network, a strategy not reported in the paper and aimed at meeting low-temperature oxidation and poisoning-resistance requirements.

fields.hypothesis: Deposit an ultrathin, porous oxygen-ion–conducting overcoat (e.g. Ce0.8Sm0.2O2–δ) by atomic layer deposition (ALD) onto the near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal element catalyst to synergistically enhance low‐temperature oxidation, poison tolerance, and long‐term durability through improved oxygen exchange with the self‐regenerative high‐entropy substrate.
fields.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic, multi-principal element automotive catalyst with a high-entropy oxide matrix that exhibits reversible exsolution/dissolution of active metallic nanoparticles under redox cycles.
fields.intervention: Apply a conformal, ultrathin (approximately 1 nm) ALD overcoat of a doped ceria (Ce0.8Sm0.2O2–δ) with controlled porosity onto the catalyst surface.
fields.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions that include transient low-temperature phases (below ~150 °C during cold-start) and long-term aging with alternating reductive/oxidative cycles in the presence of typical poisoning species (H2O, NO).
fields.structural_mediator: A nanostructured, oxygen-ion conductive overcoat that couples strongly with the high-entropy substrate to form an interfacial layer rich in mobile oxygen vacancies.
fields.mechanism: The overcoat accelerates oxygen exchange at the catalyst surface by acting as an oxygen reservoir and facilitator, thereby lowering the activation barrier for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at low temperatures. Its porous, ultrathin nature allows redox communication with the underlying high-entropy oxide, preserving the reversible exsolution/dissolution dynamics. In addition, the overcoat’s barrier properties reduce the adsorption and detrimental effects of poison species such as H2O and NO, while its oxygen storage capability helps reoxidize any over-reduced sites. This builds upon the paper's demonstration of entropy‐driven self-regeneration (PMC8505510::web::010, PMC8505510::web::015) by leveraging the dynamic oxygen vacancy network inherent in the high-entropy system.
fields.predicted_outcome: A moderate reduction in light-off temperature (expected qualitative shift toward lower temperature), improved poisoning resistance, and slower nanoparticle sintering/degradation over extended redox cycling relative to the uncoated catalyst.
fields.baseline: The unmodified high-entropy catalyst that relies solely on its intrinsic reversible exsolution/dissolution process.
fields.boundary: The overcoat thickness and porosity must be stringently controlled (targeting ~1 nm) to avoid impeding access of reactants while ensuring robust oxygen ion transport; excessively thick or dense coatings could block gas exchange.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal ALD conditions and overcoat nanostructure parameters need experimental tuning; the precise quantitative gains in activity and durability remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst sets: one set with the ALD-deposited Ce0.8Sm0.2O2–δ overcoat and a control lacking the overcoat. Subject both sets to simulated exhaust conditions featuring transient low-temperature operation and prolonged redox cycling in the presence of H2O and NO. Characterize catalytic activity, low-temperature light-off data, and nanoparticle size evolution before and after aging.
measurements: Light-off temperature for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation
Catalytic conversion rates under transient and steady-state conditions
Surface compositional analysis and nanoparticle size distribution via TEM/XRD
Resistance to performance degradation in the presence of H2O and NO
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated catalyst does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., lower light-off temperature, enhanced preservation of nanoparticle dispersion, better resistance to poisons) compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that multi-active sites and favorable electronic structures lead to enhanced catalytic performance, along with well-known properties of ceria for oxygen storage and redox activity as described in materials background.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely integrates an optimized ultrathin CeO2 overlayer with the HEA catalyst, focusing on engineering the catalyst–overlayer interface to harness interfacial charge transfer, thereby targeting a combined improvement in low-temperature reactivity, poisoning resistance, and durability for automotive exhaust applications.

fields.hypothesis: An ultrathin, conformal CeO2 overlayer deposited via atomic layer deposition (ALD) can be optimized to create an intimate interface with the near-equiatomic HEA catalyst that not only serves as an oxygen storage medium but also facilitates interfacial charge transfer to enhance low-temperature oxidation kinetics, poison resilience, and lifetime durability.
fields.material_initial_state: A uniformly mixed, near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with demonstrated high activity and fast electron transfer properties, but with potential susceptibility to transient poisoning and long-term degradation.
fields.intervention: Apply a precisely controlled ALD process to deposit an ultrathin (approximately 1–2 nm) CeO2 layer onto the HEA nanoparticles.
fields.conditions: ALD deposition performed at low temperatures (around 100–150 °C) to avoid nanoparticle sintering, followed by post-deposition treatments to ensure optimum interface formation; catalytic testing is carried out under simulated automotive exhaust conditions (including low-temperature operation below 150 °C, with H2O and NO presence) and using accelerated durability protocols.
fields.structural_mediator: A nanostructured, intimately bonded CeO2 overlayer that offers additional oxygen supply, forms favorable interfacial electronic states with the HEA, and stabilizes the surface structure against sintering and poisoning.
fields.mechanism: CeO2 is known for its high oxygen storage capacity and redox cycling, which can facilitate oxygen spillover to the active HEA sites. At the engineered interface, charge transfer occurs between the CeO2 and the underlying alloy, potentially altering the catalyst’s d-band electronic states to optimize the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates. This coupling reduces the binding strength of poisoning species and protects the catalyst against degradation under harsh automotive exhaust conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: The CeO2-coated catalyst is expected to exhibit a decreased activation barrier for low-temperature oxidation (with onset temperatures well below 150 °C), improved resistance to H2O and NO poisoning (evidenced by a shift in CO stripping profiles), and enhanced durability upon accelerated aging, relative to the uncoated HEA. The magnitude of improvement is anticipated to be moderate but significant for automotive applications.
fields.baseline: The original HEA catalyst without any oxide overlayer, which already shows high activity but may suffer from poisoning and degradation under automotive exhaust conditions.
fields.boundary: The CeO2 layer must be ultrathin and uniform; if it is too thick, it may block active sites, and if too thin or discontinuous, it may not provide sufficient oxygen buffering or protection.
fields.uncertainty: Determining the precise ALD parameters (thickness, uniformity, and interfacial bonding characteristics) required to achieve optimal performance enhancement remains an area of uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of catalysts—one with the ALD-deposited ultrathin CeO2 overlayer and a control without the coating. Characterize the interfacial structure using high-resolution TEM, XPS, and electron energy loss spectroscopy. Evaluate their performance under conditions mimicking automotive exhaust (low-temperature oxidation, H2O and NO poisoning) and after accelerated aging cycles.
measurements: Interfacial structural and electronic properties (TEM, XPS, EELS)
Onset oxidation temperature and mass activity
Poisoning resistance (e.g., shifts in CO stripping potentials)
Durability metrics (activity retention after aging cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CeO2-coated catalyst does not show significant improvements in low-temperature oxidation performance, poison resistance, and long-term durability relative to the uncoated catalyst, or if the interfacial analysis does not confirm a beneficial charge transfer interaction, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C14
top3.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that high-entropy mesoporous catalysts offer enhanced active site accessibility, extending this concept by using an ultrathin, conformal overlayer to further modify surface electronic properties and provide physical protection.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the use of a low-temperature ALD-deposited TiOxNy overlayer as a singular intervention to simultaneously tune electronic properties, prevent sintering, and resist poisoning—a strategy not reported in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: A conformal ultrathin TiOxNy overlayer deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) will tune the catalyst’s surface electronic structure, suppress poisoning species adsorption, and inhibit sintering, delivering enhanced oxidation activity, poisoning-resistance, and durability while maintaining low platinum-group-metal use.
fields.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, mesoporous multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst with a homogeneous dispersion of metals and a highly accessible pore network.
fields.intervention: Deposit a 1–2 nm thick, conformal TiOxNy layer over the entire mesoporous structure via low-temperature ALD using appropriate Ti and nitrogen precursors.
fields.conditions: Run ALD at low temperatures (≈120–150 °C) to ensure minimal thermal impact on the mesoporous architecture, followed by catalytic testing under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions (below 150 °C) with H₂O and NO poisoning as well as in accelerated thermal aging experiments.
fields.structural_mediator: The ultrathin TiOxNy overlayer forms a continuous, conformal shell on the mesoporous catalyst, selectively modifying the surface electronic states of the underlying multi-metal particles without clogging the pores.
fields.mechanism: The TiOxNy layer acts as an electronic modifier—it can shift the d-band center of the catalyst’s active sites by acting as an electron donor or acceptor—reducing the binding energy for poisoning species like NO and H₂O. Additionally, it acts as a physical barrier that retards sintering during thermal cycling while still permitting reactant diffusion due to its nanometer thickness and conformality.
fields.predicted_outcome: The modified catalyst is expected to show a reduction in the light-off temperature by approximately 10–20 °C and exhibit about a 20% higher conversion efficiency and active surface area retention after aging tests compared to the untreated catalyst.
fields.baseline: Performance of the uncoated mesoporous high-entropy catalyst evaluated under the same low-temperature exhaust environments and accelerated aging conditions.
fields.boundary: Excessively thick ALD films may block the mesoporosity and inhibit mass transport. Therefore, maintaining the ALD layer within 1–2 nm is critical.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal ALD precursors and process conditions to achieve a uniform TiOxNy layer on a complex, multi-element mesoporous surface need to be determined; minor variations in film stoichiometry may affect the predicted electronic modifications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups: one catalyst coated with a 1–2 nm TiOxNy overlayer via ALD and one uncoated. Subject both to simulated low-temperature (100–150 °C) transient exhaust conditions containing H₂O and NO and later to accelerated aging cycles. Conduct surface analytical characterization (XPS, TEM) to confirm the ALD layer’s conformality.
measurements: Light-off temperature for oxidation reactions
Conversion efficiency and poisoning resistance under low-temperature conditions
Post-aging ECSA measurement via cyclic voltammetry
Verification of ALD film thickness and conformity via XPS/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated catalyst does not exhibit at least a 10 °C reduction in light-off temperature and ≥20% improved conversion efficiency/ECSA retention relative to the uncoated catalyst (and if the ALD film is not consistently 1–2 nm), the hypothesis is falsified.
